title: Logic design
summary: The design flow, RTL to gates, timing, power and verification coverage.

ideas.how: RTL describes what a circuit does; tools work out the gates
verification takes more effort than writing the design

tradeoffs.how: raise the voltage and the clock, and watch the power climb
coverage closure: when has verification found enough?

then: Chips are drawn largely by hand, gate by gate and polygon by polygon. Verilog arrives in 1984.
Verilog (1984) lets engineers describe hardware as code; automatic logic synthesis is just arriving.
Logic synthesis and automatic place-and-route turn code into layouts.
Designing a leading-edge chip costs about ${designCost} million ({costNode}, IBS estimate).

challenges.title: Pass the slow corner
challenges.task: At a 4 GHz clock, add the fewest pipeline registers that still pass sign-off on a hot, low-voltage chip. What does it cost in latency?
challenges.hint: Choose the slow corner first. One register is enough at the typical corner, but not at the slow one.
challenges.why: Two registers pass at the slow corner, at the cost of 3 cycles of latency instead of 2. Sign-off must pass at the slow corner, because some chips will run hot at low voltage, and a design that only passes on a typical chip fails in the field.

challenges.title: Half the power
challenges.task: Start at 3 GHz and 0.75 V, about 51 W. Find the fastest clock that runs safely on less than half that power.
challenges.hint: Lower the clock, then press "Use the lowest safe voltage" each time.
challenges.why: About 2.25 GHz runs on 25 W: half the power for a quarter less speed. Power grows with voltage squared, and a slower clock lets the chip run at a lower voltage, so power falls much faster than speed. Phones and data centers both live on this trade.

challenges.title: Close coverage with an agent
challenges.task: Run 100,000 random tests and count the bugs still hiding, then let AI-guided tests try. How many tests does each need to find all 7?
challenges.hint: Run each kind of test to the end and compare the number of tests and the bugs found.
challenges.why: Random tests keep hitting the common cases, so after 100,000 runs one or two bugs in the rarest corners are usually still hiding. Guided tests aim at the bins nobody has hit and find all 7 in about 30,000. Engineers still decide what the coverage bins should be.

learn.plain: Designing a chip is like writing a huge program that turns into a city plan. Engineers write code that describes circuits, software turns it into billions of tiny switches, and checking that everything works takes longer than writing it. Every choice trades speed, power and size against each other.
learn.engineer: Static timing analysis checks setup and hold on every path across process, voltage and temperature corners with on-chip variation derates. Power sign-off covers dynamic power (αCV²f), leakage and IR drop, managed with clock gating, multiple voltage domains and dynamic voltage and frequency scaling. Verification combines UVM constrained-random simulation, formal property checking and hardware emulation, tracked by code and functional coverage.

options: Code describing what registers and logic do each clock cycle
quiz.why: Register-transfer level code, written in languages such as SystemVerilog, is what synthesis turns into gates.

quiz.q: What sets a chip's maximum clock speed?
options: The slowest logic path between flip-flops (the critical path)
quiz.why: Every path must settle within one clock period. Pipeline registers shorten the critical path.

quiz.q: Why does raising the clock frequency increase power much faster than speed?
options: Higher frequency needs higher voltage, and dynamic power grows with voltage squared
It doesn't: power grows exactly in step with speed
quiz.why: P = α·C·V²·f. Raising f also requires raising V, so power climbs steeply.
